papers.abstract: The resetting of stochastic processes has become a key mechanism appearing in many research fields, such as searching for a target, the transmission control protocol, biology, chemistry, finance, insurance, etc., with the main interest concerning the first passage time (FPT) by the process under resetting. In this paper, we focus on the exit time $\mathcal{T}_L$ from the interval $(-L, L)$ of Lévy flights (LF) under resetting, but we also consider spectrally negative Lévy processes (SNLP). As the main result, we find the asymptotics of the mean first passage time (MFPT) as $L$ tends to $+ \infty$. For LF with $α\in (0, 2)$, the scaling behaves as $L^α$ regardless of the reset rate and the asymmetry of the initial condition, a behaviour completely different from that for the known case of Brownian Motion ($α=2$). For the symmetric $α$-stable case with $α\in (0, 2)$, we also found that taking $r \to \infty$ with fixed $L$ yields a finite MFPT, which therefore may be used as a valid approximation. For completely asymmetric stable processes, we show that the scaling is very different from that for LF, and point out a method to obtain the exact distribution of FPT under resetting. The analytical calculations are verified by numerical simulations of the processes under resetting.

papers.title: Modeling electrodeposition of thin films with compact, dendritic, and random morphologies
papers.abstract: We summarize previously published computer simulation studies of a metal electrodeposition model that considers diffusive cation flux, a fast reaction in contact with the electrode or with the growing deposit, and adsorbed atom diffusion in finite time windows. Simulations with various parameters show compact, fractal, dendritic deposits, and dynamic transitions between different morphologies during the growth of individual samples. The dendritic shapes are characterized by hierarchical organizations in which branches of a given order reproduce the shape and crystalline orientation of the branches of the previous order, in contrast to the random branching of the fractal deposits formed by DLA and related models. The simulations show dendrites with maple leaf shape in SC lattices, pine tree shape in FCC lattices, and flower-like shape in HCP lattices, with surfaces predominantly oriented in the lowest-energy configurations of each lattice. Simulations with nucleation restricted to a nanoscale seed show the initial formation of faceted particles followed by dendrite formation, in agreement with silver electrodeposition on substrates patterned with gold nanoparticles. A quantitative application to faceted and dendritic silver obtained in the same experiment provides values of the model parameters which are consistent with the characteristic widths of these structures being of the same order of magnitude of the diffusion lengths of atoms on (111) and (001) surfaces. Using an extended model for iron electrodeposition on Si(100), the simulations qualitatively reproduce the initial formation of multilayer islands, small oscillations of the roughness of a polycrystalline compact film after island coalescence, and instability development. Possible directions for applying this modeling to the electrodeposition of other materials are suggested.

papers.title: Memory-resolved prediction of ligand residence times on the minutes timescale
papers.abstract: AI-enabled computational drug discovery is advancing rapidly in predicting molecular structures, binding poses and affinities, but ligand dissociation kinetics remain harder to access. Bound-state residence time, important for biological response and kinetic selectivity, is not fixed by equilibrium affinity but depends on the dissociation free-energy landscape and dissipative friction effects. Here, we show that restrained umbrella-sampling trajectories can be used to calculate residence times on the minutes timescale. Time-resolved coordinate fluctuations yield friction profiles that incorporate non-Markovian effects on dissociation kinetics. Combining them with the free-energy profile, we predict a residence time of $τ_{\rm res}$ = 275 s for the adenosine A$_{2A}$ receptor with ZM241385 (comparable to the experimental value of 125 s) and reproduce the experimental ranking of wild type and two receptor mutants. For HSP90 with compound 18 and RNase S with the S15 peptide, we predict $τ_{\rm res}$ = 2,169 s and 2,259 s (experimental values are 833 s and 2,439 s). Neglecting memory effects on residence kinetics overestimates $τ_{\rm res}$ by factors of 2.6 to 29.

papers.title: Online training of Echo State Networks to predict chaotic dynamical systems
papers.abstract: Echo State Networks (ESNs) are fundamentally important from the conceptual perspective of AI, because they provide simple and tractable frameworks for understanding temporal information processing, memory, and learning in dynamical systems. They are composed by an interconnected reservoir whose connectivity matrix remains constant over time and only the output weights are updated during the training period. In particular, ESNs employing online training allow the incremental adaptation of the output weights as data is received, making them particularly suitable for applications in which new input data becomes available over time (non-stationary environments). A key objective in the study of such learning structures is to determine which statistical properties of the reservoir enhance computational efficiency and maximize prediction performance. To this end, we investigate the effects of reservoir topology on learning performance, considering weight matrices generated from Erdos-Renyi random networks and Watts & Strogatz small-world networks. As test data we use the Lorenz and Rossler models in the chaotic regime and the FitzHugh-Nagumo model in the limit cycle regime. In the case of random Erdos-Renyi reservoirs, our simulations show that best performances are obtained for sparse reservoirs and especially when the link-density is near and immediately above the critical point of mean-field bond percolation. Watts & Strogatz reservoirs are shown to demonstrate best performance also for small values of link-density, compatible with the mean-field bond percolation when taking into account the specific nonlocal ring structure of the Watts & Strogatz reservoirs. These studies on the influence of the reservoir architecture and hyperparameters on enhancing the accuracy of ESN predictions provide an efficient framework for real-time forecasting in dynamically evolving systems.

papers.title: Absolute area under a scaled Brownian motion with resetting
papers.abstract: We investigate the statistical properties and ergodic behavior of the absolute area below the trajectory of a particle subject to stochastic resetting and moving according to a scaled Brownian motion with exponent $β$. We compare the contributions to the absolute area from the waiting times between resets and the backward recurrence time. Using the renewal formalism we derive the lower-order moments of the absolute area under both Poissonian and heavy-tailed power-law resetting waiting time distributions with exponent $α$. For Poissonian resetting, stochastic interruption suppresses fluctuations, driving the area to be ergodic, regardless of the value of $β$. In contrast, power-law resetting yields a rich spectrum of ergodic regimes. For $0 < α< 1$, the system displays weak ergodicity breaking and the maximum contribution dominates the area accumulated during the waiting times. For $1+β< α< 2$, we unveil an ergodic transition exclusive to the subdiffusive regime at $α=1+β$, where ergodicity is restored. These results clarify the subtle interplay between anomalous diffusion and power-law waiting times between resettings. Our results are tested by numerical simulations exhibiting an excellent agreement.

papers.title: Single and coupled quantum van der Pol oscillators: Wigner-function dynamics, exact qutrit solutions, and synchronization
papers.abstract: We study quantum van der Pol oscillator in which single-photon pumping competes with a nonlinear two-photon dissipative channel to produce a quantum limit cycle, and the question of how two such oscillators with non-identical intrinsic frequencies synchronize in the sense of phase locking when coupled dissipatively to one another. For a single oscillator, starting from a Lindblad description of the dynamics, we derive the exact Wigner-function evolution equation, and show that its Fokker--Planck approximation admits in the appropriate regime an equivalent classical Itô stochastic description that reproduces remarkably well the full Lindblad dynamics. Notably, the stochastic approach provides an efficient means of capturing system dynamics in the semiclassical regime, where a large number of energy eigenstates contribute and direct numerical simulations become computationally demanding. Restricting to the three lowest Fock states and using a parity symmetry, we obtain in closed form the stationary-state density matrix and its Wigner-function representation that displays pronounced nonclassical features. For two non-identical oscillators, we study the full Lindblad dynamics numerically and characterize synchronization through the stationary-state order parameter as a function of frequency mismatch and dissipative coupling. We find that increasing the effective nonlinear dissipative strength suppresses the synchronized region. Restricting the two oscillators to the three-level qutrit subspace, a parity symmetry reduces the stationary-state problem to an exact $41$-dimensional linear system, allowing to compute the synchronization order parameter. In this reduced description, results in the limit of large dissipation agree closely with those from the full dynamics, while exhibiting in the limit of small dissipation a double-peak synchronization structure accompanied by a phase reversal.

papers.title: Maximum likelihood, neural networks and posterior mean for inferring fractional Brownian motion parameters
papers.abstract: Fractional Brownian motion (fBM) is a model of anomalous diffusion parameterised by a Hurst exponent $H \in (0,1)$ and a generalised diffusion coefficient $D_H > 0$. We jointly estimate $H$ and $D_H$ using maximum likelihood (MLE) from density measurements with Poisson counting noise and single-particle trajectory with Gaussian localisation error. We show that one density measurement in time cannot infer both $H$ and $D_H$ and that several time points are needed, which matters most for inference precision. For trajectories, we show that a neural network trained with a squared error loss approximates the posterior mean of $H$, which can be computed exactly at negligible cost. Paired with the profile-likelihood estimate of $D_H$, the posterior mean has the lowest root mean squared error in both $H$ and $D_H$, except near $H=0$ and $H=1$ where MLE estimates $H$ better. In vesicle trajectories from two cell types, $H$ and $D_H$ form a continuum rather than distinct modes of motion. The posterior probability that each window within a track is subdiffusive or superdiffusive shows that $26\%$ of MRC5 fibroblast and $21\%$ of HeLa vesicle trajectories contain both subdiffusive and superdiffusive windows, against $2\%$ and $7\%$ expected from estimation uncertainty alone. Intracellular cargoes therefore switch between subdiffusion and superdiffusion over time rather than forming populations with fixed $H$.

papers.title: Understanding the Mpemba Effect through a Rule of Thumb
papers.abstract: In the Mpemba effect, a system prepared farther from equilibrium relaxes faster than one prepared closer to it. Its persistence across diverse systems, and under different dynamics of the same system, suggests that it is largely rooted in equilibrium properties, with the dynamics deciding only which mode relaxes slowest. Here we propose a simple rule of thumb for anticipating the Mpemba effect: the effect is expected when a single low-order equilibrium moment is nonmonotonic in temperature. The bath singles out this moment as the slowest to relax, so that its displacement from its bath value sets the amplitude of the slowest relaxation mode. We establish this relation exactly for low-dimensional Ornstein--Uhlenbeck processes. We then extend the rule to mean-field models by approximating their relaxation near the final equilibrium state by an Ornstein--Uhlenbeck process. For the mean-field Ising antiferromagnet, which we solve exactly in the thermodynamic limit, this approximation reproduces the main structure of the Mpemba phase diagram, including strong effects far from any phase transition. Finally, we give a general prescription for mean-field systems: identify the slowest symmetry-allowed moment of the normal coordinates at the bath, and follow its equilibrium value as a function of preparation temperature. This offers a practical route from equilibrium observables to anomalous relaxation without diagonalizing the dynamics.

papers.title: Seismology of Glasses
papers.abstract: Aging and relaxation of glasses proceed through localized rearrangements that also generate long-ranged mechanical responses in their surroundings. We develop a theory that treats these rearrangements as internal microseismic sources, and thereby separates the direct effects emerging from an event from the effects from the far-field displacements it generates. These far-field disturbances propagate and relax through the viscoelastic medium through which they move, producing a stochastic background of weak but numerous perturbations at any given location. Combining the description of local events from the Random First Order Transition theory with this propagating background, we derive a unified equation for the dynamical structure factor of a relaxing glass. The theory identifies a finite wave-vector and time window in which the growing viscoelastic far-field disturbances can produce compressed exponential relaxation, which has been observed using X-ray photon correlation spectroscopy. At higher wave vectors that resolve local jumps, heterogeneity of the local event dynamics instead produces stretched exponential relaxation. The crossover between these behaviors depends on the event statistics and the scattering phase accumulated across the region reached through viscoelastic propagation from the numerous distant sources.

papers.title: How Long Is the Coast of a Neuron? Resolution-Dependent Interaction Order and Computational Capacity
papers.abstract: Mandlebrot's coastline paradox reframes measurement as a joint property of an object and its ruler. Here we ask how observational resolution shapes the apparent structure of neural computation. We introduce a scale-indexed decomposition that separates the predictive information captured by direct dependencies from the residual outside that model family. Exact constructions show that projection can convert higher-order dependence into pairwise structure. Projection can increase the direct fraction of surviving information even as total predictive information decreases. A schematic branch-to-soma cascade grounds these effects in local coincidence detection, saturating integration and somatic mixing. Resolving organized nonlinear subunits improves approximation and raises effective representational rank. In a nested hierarchy, these gains occur without increasing information about the target. This distinction separates information availability from access by a restricted readout. A point-neuron or direct population model therefore establishes an effective description at a specified scale. It does not uniquely identify the finer computation that generated the observed relation. Which resolution is adequate depends on the observable and perturbation of interest.
